G2463.portee: For the reader, the rainbow reminds us that the invisible and divine world is very real. This magnificent natural phenomenon becomes John's language to express the inexpressible: the beauty and holiness of God's throne. Seeing a rainbow in nature can thus remind us of God's promise and his heavenly brilliance that envelops his governance.

sens: Son of Abraham and Sarah, father of Jacob and Esau
G2464.detail: 1. Isaac is the son that Abraham and his wife Sarah had in their old age, according to God's promise. His name means "he will laugh" in Hebrew, as Sarah laughed upon learning that she would bear a child despite her advanced age. He becomes the father of Jacob and Esau, and occupies a central place in the history of the people of Israel as a link between Abraham and Jacob.
G2464.origine: The Hebrew name יִצְחָק (Yitshaq) comes from a root meaning "to laugh." This name recalls both Sarah's amused disbelief and the joy of the fulfilled divine promise. Isaac represents the child of the miracle, born of a divine promise against all human expectation.
G2464.emploi: Isaac appears 18 times in the New Testament, primarily cited by the apostles and in genealogies. Matthew mentions him at the beginning of his Gospel in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:2). Mark, Luke, and Acts recall him in the confession of faith in God as the "God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" (Mark 12:26; Luke 20:37; Acts 7:32), thus affirming the continuity between God and His people. Paul uses him as an example of one who is a child of the promise (Galatians 4:28) and of faith in God (Romans 9:7-10), while the Epistle to the Hebrews praises his faith during the sacrifice commanded by God (Hebrews 11:17-20). James also mentions him as a model of faith in action (James 2:21).
G2464.portee: Isaac embodies the fundamental biblical theme of divine promise and faith. His very existence results from a word from God, reminding us that God acts against human impossibilities. For the Christian, Isaac also foreshadows the only begotten child of sacrifice, linking his story to that of Jesus. His example teaches that true descent from God is not based on flesh or human calculation, but on promise and faith.

sens: equal in nature or condition to angels
immortal and exempt from death
G2465.detail:
1. Similar to angels: the term describes those who will be "similar to angels" in their resurrected condition (Luke 20:36). It does not mean that they will become angels, but that their new state will have traits associated with angels: immortality, the absence of the need for procreation, a heavenly existence. It is a similarity of condition rather than of nature.
2. Immortal and exempt from death: since angels "cannot die anymore," those who will be resurrected will have this immunity. Jesus thus responds to the Sadducees who denied the resurrection, showing that resurrected life will be a transformed life, freed from earthly constraints.
G2465.origine: The Greek word is composed of two terms: *isos* (equal, similar) and *angelos* (angel, messenger). It therefore describes an equality or resemblance to celestial beings. This compound is simply formed to express a comparison: like the angels, to a certain extent. The word appears only once in the New Testament.
G2465.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Luke 20:36, where Jesus responds to the Sadducees who doubted the resurrection. He explains that those who will be resurrected will no longer be subject to death and will not marry, being "similar to angels." The context is a teaching on resurrection and eternal life: the condition of the resurrected will be qualitatively different from present life.
G2465.portee: This word reminds believers that resurrection is not a return to earthly life, but a profound transformation: that which will accompany the children of God into eternity. It invites us to consider not a continuation of this life, but a radical renewal, where death, the needs of the mortal body, and the structures of this present world will be removed.

sens: One of the twelve tribes of Israel
The group of descendants of Issachar, son of Jacob
G2466.detail: 1. Issachar is one of the twelve tribes of Israel, founded by Issachar, the ninth son of Jacob and Leah. In Revelation, John lists the tribes of Israel during the vision of the sealing of the 144,000: from the tribe of Issachar, twelve thousand are marked (Revelation 7:7). 2. The name also designates the entire community of the descendants of Issachar, who formed one of the divisions of the people of Israel and possessed a territory of their own in the Promised Land.
G2466.origine: The Hebrew name יִשָּׂשכָר (Issachar) literally means "there is a reward" or "reward brought," according to Leah's words at his birth in Genesis 30:18. This name reflects the mother's act of thanksgiving, who sees in this child a reward from God for giving her servant to Jacob. The tribe bears the name of its ancestor.
G2466.emploi: Issachar is one of the historical twelve tribes of Israel, founded by Jacob's son born of Leah. In the New Testament, the name appears only once, in Revelation 7:7, where John cites the tribes during his eschatological vision. This unique mention underscores the importance of continuity between ancient Israel and the final vision of God's plan.
G2466.portee: The sealing of Issachar, like that of the other tribes, reminds us of God's faithfulness to His people and His covenant with the descendants of Jacob. This vision reveals that God protects and marks His people at the end of times, offering believers the assurance that the divine purpose encompasses the entire history of Israel and unfolds until its completion.

sens: To know by experience or direct knowledge
To be known, recognizable to someone
G2467.detail:
1. This verb means to know something or someone through lived experience or direct perception. It is a knowledge that comes from practice or observation—not just information heard. In Acts 26:4, Paul states that his life from his youth "is known by all the Jews": it is not a rumor, but a reality they themselves could verify, as he lived in Jerusalem among them.
2. The word can also express the idea of being known, visible, recognizable—what is public and notorious. This is the passive side: something is not hidden, but manifest to all.
G2467.origine: This Greek verb belongs to the family of words related to vision and perception. The form encountered in the New Testament is primarily the perfect tense with present value, making it a state verb rather than an action verb: it describes a state of established and lasting knowledge. The word often translates the Hebrew from the Old Testament that expresses knowledge through direct experience.
G2467.emploi: This verb appears only once in Acts 26:4, in Paul's speech before King Agrippa. Paul relies on what everyone in Jerusalem can testify: his past life is known to all, as it unfolded before their eyes. It is a call to public testimony and collective memory: Paul's life is not a mystery, but an established and observable reality.
G2467.portee: This word reminds us that true knowledge is not reduced to words or assertions. It rests on observable facts and shared experience. When Paul says that his former life is "known," he invites his listeners to judge based on evidence: his transformation in Christ is not a hidden matter, but visible to those who truly know him.

sens: Disciple of Jesus among the twelve apostles
The one who betrayed Jesus to the Jewish authorities
Name also associated with the father of Judas
G2469.detail:
1. Iscariot is the nickname of Judas, one of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus. This name identifies and distinguishes him from the other disciples, notably another apostle named Jude (Luke 6:16). This is how the Bible consistently refers to him in all the gospels.

2. The word is inseparable from betrayal: Judas Iscariot is "the one who delivered Jesus" (Mark 3:19). He negotiated with the religious leaders to help them arrest Jesus in exchange for money (Matthew 26:14), an act that the Bible presents as inspired by Satan himself (Luke 22:3).

3. The name also applies to the father of Judas, Simon Iscariot (John 6:71), thus designating a common lineage or origin.
G2469.origine: The word likely comes from the Hebrew "Qiryah Ish" or a similar expression, meaning a link to a city or locality. It is not a family name in the modern sense, but rather a nickname or designation that connects the person to a place. This origin remains debated among scholars, but it underscores that the nickname had a concrete meaning for the early readers of the Gospel.
G2469.emploi: Iscariot appears in the four gospels about 11 times, always attached to the name of Judas, and once to the name of Simon his father (John 6:71). In the lists of the apostles (Matthew 10:4, Mark 3:19, Luke 6:16), he is systematically named and characterized as the one who delivered Jesus. As the narrative progresses, the nickname reminds the reader of the identity of the traitor: during the preparation for Passover (Matthew 26:14, Mark 14:10), during his arrest (John 13:2), and during the meal with Jesus (John 12:4, John 13:26). The context shows that the nickname was already established and known, serving to unambiguously identify the unfaithful disciple.
G2469.portee: The name Iscariot reminds the believer that even among those whom Jesus chose and directly taught, betrayal occurred. It is a warning about the reality of human free will and the power of evil to corrupt; Judas was not forced but chose to deliver Jesus. For the reader of the Gospels, this nickname embodies a lesson in humility and spiritual vigilance: it invites one to examine their own faithfulness to Jesus and not to assume that proximity to Christ guarantees perseverance.

sens: Of the same size, number, or quantity
Of the same nature or quality
Having the same rank, value
Identical, similar
Fair, just
G2470.detail:
1. Equal in the sense of the same dimension or quantity: two things that have exactly the same size, number, or measure. In Matthew 20:12, the workers who worked all day protest receiving the same wage as those who worked only one hour: treating equally means granting the same remuneration.
2. Equal in the sense of accorded, identical in facts or testimonies: two elements that correspond, that agree. In Mark 14:56 and 14:59, the false testimonies against Jesus did not agree — they were not equal to each other, not consistent.
3. Equal in the sense of the same rank or status: to place oneself at the same level as another person. In John 5:18, Jesus makes himself equal to God: he claims to have the same rank, the same divine authority.
4. Equal used adverbially or in the neuter plural to mean "the same thing": in Luke 6:34, to give back (literally "the same things") means to act in the same way.
5. Equal in the sense of identical gift or equivalent grace: in Acts 11:17, the same gift refers to a blessing of the same nature and value granted to all believers.
G2470.origine: The Greek word ἴσος comes from a root expressing equality and balance. It often translates the Hebrew אֶחָד ("one", "unique") and כְּ ("like", "according to"), words that express identity or conformity. The family of the word includes derivatives for equality, justice, and balance. It is a fundamental word to express not only quantitative resemblance but also moral fairness.
G2470.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament according to these uses. It is used in very varied contexts: remuneration (Matthew 20:12), concordance of testimonies (Mark 14:56, 59), commercial exchange (Luke 6:34), the divine nature of Jesus (John 5:18), the distribution of spiritual gifts (Acts 11:17), and celestial dimensions (Revelation 21:16). Its meaning varies according to the context: sometimes equal strictly means identical in quantity, sometimes it expresses concordance or agreement, sometimes an identity of nature or rank. The most theologically rich use is John 5:18, where Jesus is described as equating himself with God — that is, claiming the same authority and divinity.
G2470.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on justice and fairness: God treats his children with radical equality, not based on merit but on grace. In John 5:18, Jesus' equality with God reveals who he truly is and establishes trust in his saving power. The word also reminds us that in the body of Christ, the gifts of the Spirit are generously given impartially to all believers.

sens: State where everyone has the same share, the same portion
Fair and impartial treatment, without favoritism
G2471.detail:
1. In the literal sense, equality is when the portions or shares are the same for all. In 2 Corinthians 8:14, Paul speaks of equality between rich and poor Christians: the one who has much gives so that the one who has little lacks nothing, and together they are brought to equality, to parity of situation.
2. In the sense of fairness or justice, it is treating each person impartially and appropriately to their condition. In Colossians 4:1, the Christian master must grant his servants what is just and fair—not equal in every sense, but proportionate and honest, what is rightfully theirs.
G2471.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἴσος (isos, "equal"), which expresses the idea of parity or correspondence between two things. The root evokes a balance, an equilibrium: each has their share without tilting to one side. The equivalent Hebrew word in the Old Testament would be related to the idea of "right" and "equal measure."
G2471.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's epistles. In 2 Corinthians 8:14, it concerns material assistance among Christians: generosity creates a practical equality, a solidarity. In Colossians 4:1, it pertains to the master-servant relationship: equity here means not the abolition of roles, but the fair application of each one's rights, recognizing that the master has a heavenly master. In these two contexts, Paul uses the word to remind that Christian life requires impartiality of heart.
G2471.portee: Biblical equality is not a political abstraction, but a concrete virtue: sharing generously, treating each person justly according to their condition, and recognizing that all Christians—rich and poor, masters and servants—are equal before God. It is a call to honesty of heart in our relationships.

sens: Who has the same worth, the same dignity as another thing
Of equal importance or merit
Equal in honor or esteem
G2472.detail:
1. The word literally designates what has the same monetary or material value: two things that cost the same, that are worth the same. In 2 Peter 1:1, the "faith of equal value" means a faith as precious, as esteemed as that of the apostles — not a faith of lesser value, but fully equal in spiritual dignity.
2. By extension, this concerns the honor, consideration, esteem one enjoys: receiving an equal share of honor or respect. The Christians Peter speaks of are not second-class believers: they enjoy the same spiritual dignity as the apostles themselves.
3. It is a radical affirmation of equality: despite differences in functions or roles in the Church, all believers receive the same faith, the same price of esteem before God.
G2472.origine: The Greek word is composed of two parts: *isos* (equal, alike) and *timè* (price, value, honor, esteem). It is a comparative adjective that emphasizes exact equivalence. The *timè* in the Bible covers both material value and social or spiritual honor, allowing the word to express not only equality of price but equality of esteem and dignity.
G2472.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 1:1. Peter uses it to address the scattered Christians and to affirm that their faith — although they did not accompany Jesus in the flesh like the apostles — is no less valuable than that of the apostles themselves. It is a word of consolation and affirmation: it assures readers that their spiritual position is as solid, as honorable, as precious as that of the first eyewitnesses of the resurrection.
G2472.portee: This word reminds Christians of a fundamental truth: faith has only one price before God, whether you are an apostle or a simple believer. It comforts and encourages those who are not major figures: you have received a faith of equal dignity, the same access to God, the same esteem. It is an affirmation of the essential equality of all believers in the Church of Christ.

sens: who shares the same feelings and convictions
who thinks and feels in the same way
who has their spirit aligned with another
G2473.detail:
1. This word describes someone who thinks, feels, and engages like another person. In Philippians 2:20, Paul says he has no one "of the same mind" to sincerely care for the situation of the Philippians: he seeks someone who shares his apostolic passion and love for this church.
2. The image is of two souls beating in the same rhythm, having the same orientation of heart. It is not merely a shared intellectual opinion, but a deep communion of feelings and concerns.
3. It is the opposite of division or indifference: it is the unity of heart and thought that a leader (like an apostle) seeks in those who work with him.
G2473.origine: The word combines two Greek roots: ἴσος (equal) and ψυχή (soul, heart, life). Its basic image is that of souls or hearts "equal" or "aligned". This composition reflects the importance that Greek thought attributes to inner agreement in communal life. In biblical Hebrew, a similar notion appears in expressions of brotherly communion, although the Greek isopsuchos is a specifically Greek creation to express this harmony of soul.
G2473.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: Philippians 2:20. Paul uses it to characterize the type of help he seeks to care for the Philippians. The rarity of the word shows that it is a carefully chosen term, very expressive: Paul does not simply want someone who obeys, but someone who thinks and feels like him, driven by the same devotion to Christ and to his church.
G2473.portee: This word invites Christians to seek not only colleagues or friends, but brothers and sisters "of the same mind" — that is, who share their faith, their passion for Jesus, and their love for others. It is a call to deep unity, beyond mere superficial agreements. Paul teaches us that true spiritual collaboration requires this communion of heart and mind.

sens: The chosen people of God, descendants of Jacob
The nation and territory inhabited by this people
The entirety of the twelve tribes descended from Jacob's sons
All members of this people, considered collectively
The believers in Jesus, heirs of the promises made to Israel
G2474.detail:
1. Israel primarily designates the people that God chose and established to be His special people. The name comes from Jacob, who received it after wrestling with God (Genesis 32:28), which means "he who wrestles with God." Jesus says of the centurion: "I have not found such great faith in Israel" (Matthew 8:10), referring to the people of Israel as a whole.
2. Israel can also refer to the territory, the land that God gave to this people to inhabit. When speaking of "the land of Israel" or "the land of Judah," it evokes this geographical space, as in Matthew 2:20-21 where the angel commands Joseph: "Get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel."
3. In some passages, Israel refers to the twelve tribes, the various clans that make up the people. In Matthew 19:28, Jesus promises His apostles that they "will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel."
4. The word can also simply refer to the people as a whole, at a given time. When we read "Jesus spoke to the crowd" or "John had preached a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel" (Acts 13:24), it speaks of the Israelites living at that moment.
5. In the New Testament, Paul applies the name Israel to Christian believers, heirs of the promises: "Peace be upon them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God" (Galatians 6:16), showing that believers in Jesus become the true spiritual Israel.
G2474.origine: The word Israel comes from the Hebrew יִשְׁרָאֵל (Genesis 32:28), where Jacob receives this name after wrestling all night with God: it literally means "he who wrestles with God" or "God wrestles." It is the foundational name of the entire people descended from this man. In the Greek Old Testament, this name is always retained in this Hebrew form, transliterated into Greek as Ἰσραήλ. The name thus evokes from the beginning an intimate relationship with God, not a passive submission, but a covenant made through struggle and faith.
G2474.emploi: Israel appears 68 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels and Paul's Epistles. In the Gospels, Jesus speaks of Israel as the people for whom He was first sent (Matthew 10:6: "Go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel"). Acts describes the people of Israel at the time of Pentecost and the initial apostolic preaching (Acts 4:10). Paul extensively discusses the status of Israel in relation to the Gospel: Israel according to the flesh (1 Corinthians 10:18) rejected Jesus, but God has not rejected His people (Romans 11:2). The word designates both the historical and fleshly people, as well as the spiritual Israel of believers. Its usage nuances according to context: political and nationalistic when Jesus' enemies demand that He come down from the cross as "king of Israel" (Matthew 27:42), theological when Paul discusses salvation and the promise made to Israel (Romans 11:26).
G2474.portee: Israel is at the heart of biblical thought on salvation. The New Testament affirms that God has not abandoned Israel despite the rejection of Jesus by many (Romans 11:2), and that salvation, although first offered to the Israelites, extends to all peoples. The Christian discovers here that God's promises to Israel also concern all who believe in Jesus, who become the true Israel. Understanding what the Bible says about Israel helps the believer grasp their own status in God's plan.

sens: Member of the people of Israel, descendant of Jacob
One who belongs to God's chosen people and heir of divine promises
Person of sincerity and moral integrity in their faith
G2475.detail:
1. An Israelite is a member of the people of Israel, descended from Jacob and his lineage. It is a national and religious status: Acts uses it to refer to the Jews as a people, as when Peter says, "Men of Israel, listen to these words" (Acts 2:22).
2. The word primarily evokes the theocratic privilege, that is, the special covenant between this people and God. Paul proudly reminds us: "Israelites, to whom belongs the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, the worship, and the promises" (Romans 9:4).
3. Jesus also praises its spiritual sincerity: upon seeing Nathanael, he says, "Here truly is an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit" (John 1:47), linking the name to the absence of deceit and to the uprightness of heart.
G2475.origine: The Greek word comes directly from the name Israel (Ἰσραήλ), which means "God fights" or "one who struggles with God" — an allusion to Jacob wrestling with the divine angel (Genesis 32). The suffix -ite marks belonging to this people. The form thus naturally designates "one who belongs to Israel," claiming the heritage of the patriarch and his covenant with God.
G2475.emploi: The term appears 9 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Acts and Paul's epistles. In Acts, it serves to respectfully address the Jewish people in the heart of Jerusalem — apostles and preachers use it as a title of honor to address their brethren (Acts 2:22, 3:12, 5:35, 13:16, 21:28). Paul uses it to assert his religious status and rights within the chosen people (Romans 9:4, 11:1, 2 Corinthians 11:22). John places it in the mouth of Jesus evaluating moral sincerity (John 1:47). The meaning remains constant: it is never a mere ethnic name, but always carries the prestige of the divine covenant.
G2475.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that the Church inherits the promises made to Israel. Understanding that the early apostles proudly claimed the title of Israelite shows how the Gospel is rooted in the history of the chosen people and does not deny it. It is also an invitation to spiritual sincerity: Jesus praises the Israelite "without deceit," calling his disciples to an honest faith devoid of pretense.

sens: To occupy a vertical position, to be upright on one's feet
To be present in a place, to be there
To take a position in front of someone or something
To subsist, to endure, to remain stable
To be established, founded, instituted (figurative sense)
To remain firm, to persevere in faith or in a moral position
G2476.detail:
1. To stand: the most concrete meaning. John was standing there with his disciples (John 1:35), a woman stood at his feet weeping (Luke 7:38), the star stopped above the place where the child was (Matthew 2:9).
2. To be present, to be found in a place: this nuance emphasizes less the posture than the presence. A man was there who had a withered hand (Luke 6:8), the healed man stood near them (Acts 4:14).
3. To present oneself, to appear before someone: implies a confrontation, a coming into presence. The servant stood at the door waiting (Luke 12:37), and especially: he stands at the door and knocks (Revelation 3:20).
4. To subsist, to remain: the idea that something persists, stays in place. A house divided against itself cannot stand (Matthew 12:25).
5. To be established, instituted, founded (figurative sense): the word describes what is put in place, instituted. Jesus says: I appoint you as a minister and a witness (Acts 26:16).
6. To remain firm morally or spiritually: to be unwavering in faith. Stand firm in grace (Romans 5:2), it is an image of moral and spiritual stability in the face of temptations.
G2476.origine: The Greek verb ἵστημι (histêmi) comes from an Indo-European root meaning to place or put in position. It is a very productive verb: it expresses the action of putting upright (transitive sense) but also the act of standing (intransitive sense). In Greek, the perfect and pluperfect have a present sense: one who has stood remains standing. In the Greek Old Testament, the word primarily translates the Hebrew עמד (ʿamad, to stand) and קוּם (qoum, to rise, to stand).
G2476.emploi: This verb is very frequent in the New Testament: 151 occurrences. It appears everywhere — in the four Gospels, Acts, Paul's epistles, Revelation. In the literal sense, it describes physical postures and presences: the star stops (Matthew 2:9), the disciples stand near the cross (Luke 23:49), the resurrected one suddenly appears among them (John 20:19). In the figurative sense, very important in Paul, it expresses spiritual stability: to stand firm in faith (Romans 11:20), to stand firm by putting on the armor of God (Ephesians 6:11). The nuance varies according to the context: physical presence, appearance, subsistence, moral firmness.
G2476.portee: This verb speaks to the Christian of two essential things. First, it shows that our presence matters: it is by standing firm in the face of temptation, by remaining where God places us, that we bear witness (Acts 26:16). Secondly, it reveals that the Christian faith is not passive: it requires standing firm, remaining steadfast in grace and truth, being unshakeable. The image of standing evokes the responsibility and vigilance of the believer.

sens: To visit someone to meet and get to know them
To seek to know, to inquire from someone
G2477.detail:
1. The verb primarily means "to visit" someone with the aim of meeting and creating a personal connection. It is the idea of spending time with someone to gradually get to know them. Paul uses it in Galatians 1:18 when he says he went up to Jerusalem "to get acquainted with Cephas": it was about meeting Peter, spending time with him for fifteen days to establish a relationship and exchange on faith.

2. More broadly, the verb can mean "to inquire from someone" or "to seek to know something" by asking questions. It is an active approach to learn what one does not know.
G2477.origine: The verb comes from the Greek "histôr," which means "one who knows" or "one who has seen." It is from the same family as the French word "histoire" (from the Greek "historia"). Originally, it designates inquiry and the account of what one has learned by questioning witnesses or visiting places. The word thus evokes the idea of acquiring knowledge through direct observation and personal contact.
G2477.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament as we have it, in Galatians 1:18. Paul uses it to describe his visit to Jerusalem three years after his conversion, in order to meet Cephas (Peter). The context shows that it is not just about passing through the city, but about deliberately seeking to establish a personal relationship and to get to know this key apostle of the Church. The verb thus emphasizes the personal and intentional nature of this meeting.
G2477.portee: This word reminds us that getting to know someone in faith does not happen at a distance. Paul deemed it important to go up to Jerusalem to meet Peter face to face, even long after his conversion. For the believer, this invites valuing fraternal meetings and direct sharing with other Christians: community is built through presence and personal exchange, not just theory.

sens: Having great physical or muscular strength.
Having great power, a great capacity for action or influence.
Intense, vigorous, striking.
Imposing, large in size or importance.
When speaking of God, possessing absolute and unsurpassed power.
G2478.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes remarkable physical strength: a strong man in battle can bind an opponent, just as he can plunder a house (Mark 3:27). John the Baptist says that the one who comes after him is "more powerful" than he (Matthew 3:11), referring to a superiority that goes beyond mere muscular strength.

2. It applies to general power of action: a "great" famine (that is, intense and devastating) ravages a country (Luke 15:14). Paul's epistles are described as "strong" in content (2 Corinthians 10:10).

3. A "strong" voice, a "loud" cry, or a "strong" exhortation marks intensity and effectiveness (Hebrews 5:7). The warriors who shut the mouths of lions or quenched the power of fire were "valiant" in battle (Hebrews 11:34).

4. The word fits what is large and imposing: a "mighty" angel descends from heaven with signs of majesty (Revelation 10:1), or a "strong" fortified city.

5. Applied to God, "strong" asserts His absolute power against which no human power can compete (1 Corinthians 10:22). God's "weakness" remains stronger than men (1 Corinthians 1:25).
G2478.origine: The word comes from the verb ἰσχύω, which means "to have strength, to be able." In Hebrew, it often translates terms like אֵל (El, strength, god), גִּבּוֹר (gibor, mighty warrior) or חָזַק (hazaq, to be strong, to strengthen). This family of words evokes a concrete and visible power, that of a warrior, a fortress, or a storm.
G2478.emploi: The word appears 27 times in the New Testament, mainly in Revelation and the epistles. It primarily describes powerful men in battle or of great authority (Hebrews 11:34, Revelation 6:15: the rich and the powerful). It then qualifies celestial beings, angels or resurrected ones, whose power surpasses that of humans (Revelation 10:1). It applies to intense realities: a famine, a voice, an epistle (Luke 15:14, Hebrews 5:7). Finally, it characterizes the power of God and Christ, unfathomable and unsurpassable (1 Corinthians 10:22, Revelation 18:8). In the Gospels, John the Baptist uses this term to magnify the one who comes after him.
G2478.portee: This word invites the Christian to recognize the different forms of power: that of man, limited and subject to sin, and that of God, absolute and irresistible. It encourages not to fear the strength of the world or its adversaries, but to place trust in the omnipotence of God. For the believer, it reminds that even weakness in Christ surpasses all human wisdom.

sens: Physical or moral capacity to produce an effect, to resist, to act.
Power in action, deployed vigor.
Energy or resources of the soul.
Divine strength or power of God.
G2479.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes physical or moral strength: the concrete capacity to act, to endure, to accomplish. It is the vigor that enables someone to do something. When Jesus commands us to love God "with all [our] strength" (Mark 12:30), He asks us to put all our energy, all our life commitment into it.
2. Ischus can also mean power in action, manifested and effective strength, that which produces results. Ephesians 1:19 speaks of the greatness of God's power "being effectively manifested by the virtue of His strength" — God does not have inactive strength, but a strength that operates.
3. The word is used for the inner resources of the soul: Luke 10:27 lists the heart, soul, strength, and mind, showing that strength is a deep dimension of our being, not only muscular but spiritual and voluntary.
4. Ischus also denotes divine power, God's strength in His majesty. In Revelation 5:12, the "strength" of the resurrected Christ is proclaimed; in 2 Thessalonians 1:9, "the glory of His strength" evokes the formidable power of the Lord at judgment.
G2479.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes solidity, vigor, the capacity to hold and resist. In Greek, it is distinct from "dynamis" (power in general, capacity) and "kratos" (dominion, mastery): ischus emphasizes strength as resource or energy. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew "koakh" (vital force) and also "khayil" (strength, army, virtue), "oz" (raw strength), and "gvourah" (power, valor): all words that express a concrete and active strength.
G2479.emploi: The word appears 10 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Epistles and Revelation. It is particularly frequent in Jesus' words about the love of God (Mark 12, parallel Luke 10): to love God "with all one's strength" means to give oneself without reserve. Paul uses it to speak of God's power at work in us (Ephesians 1:19, 6:10) and to exhort believers to be strengthened in the Lord. In Revelation, ischus glorifies the power of Christ in heaven. The context is often that of divine power, spiritual energy, or the total commitment of the believer.
G2479.portee: This word reminds the believer that true strength is not primarily physical, but encompasses our entire being — heart, soul, mind, and will. To love God "with all one's strength" means to give Him what is most intense and alive within us. Conversely, the believer is called to "be strengthened in the Lord" (Ephesians 6:10): it is an invitation to draw strength not from oneself, but from the divine power that works within him.

sens: To be in good physical health, to be well
To have the strength, the ability to do something
To be powerful, to dominate, to prevail
To be effective, to produce the expected result
To be able to resist, to endure
G2480.detail:
1. To have good physical health and be robust: this is the state of one who is not sick. In Mark 2:17, Jesus distinguishes those who "are well" from the sick who need a physician.

2. To have the capacity, strength, or power to accomplish an action: this means to be able to do something concretely. Thus in John 21:6, the disciples "could not" draw the net full of fish. In Luke 14:29, it is asked whether someone "can" finish what he has started.

3. To be powerful, to dominate or to conquer: this means to have the strength to impose one's will or to resist. In Acts 19:20, "the word of the Lord grew in power," it gained ground. In Revelation 12:8, the dragon "could not" defeat the Church.

4. To be useful, to serve a purpose, to produce the expected effect: this is the effectiveness of something. In Matthew 5:13, salt that has lost its flavor "is no longer good for anything." In Galatians 5:6, circumcision "is of no value" without faith.

5. To be able to resist, to stand firm in the face of a trial: this means to have solidity or endurance. In Luke 6:48, a house well built on the rock "could not" be shaken by a flood.
G2480.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ἰσχύς (strength, power). In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew חָזַק (to be strong, to strengthen), גִּבּוֹר (to be powerful, to be a hero), and עָצַם (to be strong, to strengthen). It is an action verb that describes the state or condition of one who possesses strength, whether physical or moral.
G2480.emploi: This verb appears 28 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It is used for very varied realities: physical health (Mark 2:17), the ability to accomplish an action (Luke 8:43, Acts 6:10), power and effectiveness (Acts 19:20), the resistance of a structure (Luke 6:48), or the usefulness of something (Matthew 5:13, Galatians 5:6). The context changes the meaning: with an infinitive, it means "to be able to do"; with an accusative of a person, it means "to conquer or dominate someone" (Acts 19:16). In Hebrews 9:17, a testament "is of force" only if the one who made it has died. The verb thus expresses a capacity, an effectiveness, or a strength that is exercised.
G2480.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on true power: it does not reside in us, but in God. Philippians 4:13 affirms that we can "do all things" through Christ who "strengthens" us. In Acts 19:20, the growth of the Church is not due to human persuasion, but to the power of the word of God. This term also urges us to seek where our true strength lies and to recognize our human limits, like the disciples in the face of the storm or the young man terrified by evil spirits.

sens: Equally, with the same chance or probability
With doubt or uncertainty; it may be that
G2481.detail:
1. The word primarily expresses an equality of chances: two things have the same weight, the same probability. This is the image of the Greek word itself, which comes from a root meaning "equal."
2. From this comes the sense of doubt or uncertainty: when the master of the vineyard sends his son, he wonders "perhaps they will respect him" (Luke 20:13) — he does not know if this will happen, he hopes for an equal outcome between two possibilities, without certainty.
G2481.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning "equal" (ἴσος, isos). Its primary meaning, "equally," has expanded to express uncertainty: when two outcomes have equal weight, one does not know which will occur. This is why "perhaps" is the best translation. The Greek word translates Hebrew adverbs such as אוּלַי (oulai) or אַךְ (ak), which also carry this nuance of uncertainty or possibility.
G2481.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 20:13, in the parable of the vineyard workers. Jesus tells how the master of the vineyard sends his son, wondering "perhaps" the vineyard workers will respect him — it is a fragile expectation, a hope without guarantee. The context shows that it is precisely this uncertainty that dramatizes the scene: the master has no certainty, he only hopes.
G2481.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that true faith does not arise from calculation or human certainty: it rests on hope in God despite the uncertainty of the world. In this parable, the son sent "perhaps" will be respected — but of course, he is rejected. This calls us to place our trust not in our fragile predictions, but in the faithfulness of God who acts beyond our expectations.

sens: Large Mediterranean country in southern Europe, located west of Greece
Region of capital importance for the expansion of early Christianity
G2482.detail:
1. Italy is the vast territory in southern Europe, bordered by the Mediterranean, where the city of Rome is located and whose inhabitants are Italians. It is the heart of the Roman Empire at the time of the New Testament. Aquila and Priscilla came from there (Acts 18:2), and several ships sailed to this country (Acts 27:1, 27:6).
2. For the early Christians, Italy is the land to which the message of the Gospel spreads: Paul himself, as a prisoner, is sent there to appear before Caesar (Acts 27:1), and Christians from Italy greet the recipients of the letter to the Hebrews (Hebrews 13:24), showing that the Church has taken root there despite persecutions.
G2482.origine: The Greek word "Italy" comes from Latin, like many geographical names in the New Testament. The country likely derives its name from ancient Italic peoples. The Romans call this peninsula their political and military center, and it is there that Paul aspires to testify, as he declared before his capture (see Romans 1:13-15).
G2482.emploi: The word "Italy" appears four times in the New Testament, only in Acts and the letter to the Hebrews. In Acts, it is the destination of decisive journeys: Aquila returns from there (18:2), and Paul is sent there as a prisoner to be judged (27:1, 27:6). In Hebrews 13:24, Christians from Italy send their greetings, a sign that the Christian community has established itself there. The context is always that of the spread of the Gospel and the presence of a living Church in the heart of the empire.
G2482.portee: Italy in the New Testament symbolizes the universal reach of the Gospel: not only does the early Church extend to the political center of the known world, but it thrives enough to send its greetings to other churches. Paul's captivity on the way to Italy also reminds us that nothing can stop the progression of the Word, not even the imprisonment of an apostle.

sens: belonging to Italy or originating from it
G2483.detail: 1. The Italian Cohort was a Roman military unit stationed at Caesarea in Palestine. The centurion Cornelius was its commander (Acts 10:1). The word simply designates what comes from Italy or what depends on it — here a troop of Roman soldiers from Italy or organized according to the Italian military structure.
G2483.origine: The word comes from the name of Italy (Ἰταλία in Greek). At the time of the New Testament, Italy was the heart of the Roman Empire, and everything that was "Italian" was associated with the political and military power of Rome. The Greek uses the suffix -ικός (which means "of" or "related to") to make it an adjective.
G2483.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 10:1, where the apostle Peter meets Cornelius, centurion of the Italian Cohort at Caesarea. This context shows that direct Roman troops, coming from Italy or organized in the Italian manner, were present in the Holy Land to maintain order and the authority of Rome. It is a historical detail that situates the action within the framework of Roman occupation.
G2483.portee: This mention reminds us that the Gospel has spread even among the Roman occupiers themselves. Cornelius, although a foreigner to Israel and a soldier of an invading empire, is presented as a devout man who fears God and prays — a lesson on God's grace that transcends national and political boundaries.

sens: mountain region of Syria northeast of Palestine
G2484.detail: 1. Iturea is a mountainous region located in Syria, northeast of the Promised Land. It is a little-known but very real territory in the geography of the ancient Middle East. It appears in the Gospel as a distinct territory, placed under the authority of a tetrarch (a governor of lower rank) during the time of Jesus.
G2484.origine: The name comes from the people of the Itureans, an Aramean tribe established in this mountainous region of Syria. The inhabitants of Iturea were called the Itureans. The Greek name Ἰτουραῖος reflects the designation of the people and the territory they occupied in antiquity.
G2484.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:1, when Luke lists the governors of the various territories in the region at the time John the Baptist begins his ministry. Iturea is mentioned there as one of the tetrarchies (regions governed by a tetrarch), placed under the authority of Philip, the half-brother of King Herod. This enumeration geographically and politically situates the context of Jesus' arrival and the beginning of John the Baptist's preaching.

sens: A young fish or a small-sized fish
A modest food offered or eaten in small quantities
G2485.detail:
1. The word refers to a small fish or a young fish, in contrast to a large fish. It is a diminutive of the ordinary word for fish, which conveys affection or the impression of smallness. In Matthew 15:34, in the account of the multiplication of the loaves, Jesus asks the disciples: "How many loaves do you have? Seven, they replied, and a few small fish" — these small fish are listed alongside the seven loaves to make up the meal.
2. On a concrete and social level, the small fish is a humble food that can be given in small quantities. Mark 8:7 reports the same miracle: "They had a few small fish, and Jesus, having given thanks, had them also distributed." These small fish are among the limited resources that the disciples gather, which Jesus blesses and multiplies to feed the hungry crowd.
G2485.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἰχθύς (ichthus, "fish") with the addition of a diminutive suffix (-ίδιον) that expresses smallness or affection. This suffix creates a tone of tenderness or familiarity around the word. The Greek uses this process to show not only that we are talking about small fish but also to create a certain closeness with these creatures — they are called as one would speak of a small child.
G2485.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in the two accounts of the multiplication of the loaves: Matthew 15:34 and Mark 8:7. In these two parallel passages, the small fish play the same role: they are the modest food resources that the disciples possess, listed alongside the loaves. Jesus takes these fish, gives thanks, and has them distributed to the crowd. The fact that these fish are described as "small" emphasizes the material insufficiency of the means at hand — a few small fish in the face of a multitude — and makes the miraculous power of Jesus, who feeds all the people, even more visible.
G2485.portee: These small fish remind us that God works from what we have, even if it seems trivial or insignificant. The disciples bring little: a few loaves and a few small fish. It is the trust in Jesus and His blessing that transforms this modesty into abundance for the multitude. This image invites Christians not to despise the small things they can offer or possess, but to surrender them to God, knowing that His power can do much more than our human calculations would imagine.

sens: Aquatic animal with fins and scales, living in fresh or salt water
Common food, a staple for the table
Figuratively in parables: what the benevolent father gives to the one who asks
G2486.detail:
1. The fish is primarily an ordinary aquatic animal, one that fishermen catch in their nets. John recounts how the disciples "drew the net full of fish" after the resurrection of Jesus (John 21:8), which shows the richness of a miraculous catch. It is a concrete, material word.
2. As food, fish plays an important role in the Gospel: Jesus multiplies the loaves and the fish to feed the crowd (Mark 6:41), thus demonstrating His compassion. The disciples also share it, highlighting that fish was a common and acceptable food at the time.
3. In Jesus' parables, fish becomes a moral image: the father who loves his children will not give them a serpent instead of a fish (Matthew 7:10; Luke 11:11). Here, fish represents something good and useful, in contrast to what would be bad or dangerous. It is the just gift of a loving father.
G2486.origine: The Greek word ichthus comes from the same realm as the Hebrew word *dag*, which also means fish. The root simply evokes the aquatic animal, without hidden imagery. The word later became engraved in Christian memory because the Greek letters of ichthus (ΙΧΘΥΣ) form the acrostic "Jesus Christ Son of God Savior," but this acrostic was not a meaning of the word itself at the time of the New Testament.
G2486.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and once in Paul. It always refers to a real fish or a group of fish. In the accounts of the multiplication of loaves (Matthew 14:19, Mark 6:41, Luke 9:16), the fish accompany the loaves as elements of the miracle. In the fishing scenes (Luke 5:6-9, John 21:6-11), it is the abundance of the catch that draws attention. In Jesus' parables (Matthew 7:10, Luke 11:11), fish is the example of a good and useful gift. The word does not vary in its fundamental meaning: it is always the same animal or food, seen sometimes as a resource from fishing, sometimes as food, sometimes as a symbol of good in a comparison.
G2486.portee: The fish in the Gospel speaks to us of God's providence that provides for bodily needs, and of the miracles of Jesus that transform the little into abundance. But it also speaks primarily of the generosity of the Father: when we ask, He does not deceive us by giving us something bad, but He satisfies our sincere request. It is an assurance of trust: God never abandons us in our needs.

sens: Imprint, mark left by the passage of a person or an animal
Path or route followed while walking
Figuratively: example to imitate, model of conduct
G2487.detail: 1. The word trace primarily refers to the concrete imprint left by a foot or paw: it is the image of a traveler who has left their marks on the ground while passing. 2. It then signifies the road itself, the path one follows while walking in the footsteps of someone else — the idea of walking in the same traces means walking in the same place, in the same way. 3. Figuratively, a trace becomes an example to imitate, a model of conduct: "to follow in someone's traces" means to imitate them, to reproduce their life and actions. It is in this sense that the apostle Peter exhorts believers to "follow in the traces" of Christ in His suffering (1 Peter 2:21), and Paul speaks of those who "walk in the traces" of Abraham's faith (Romans 4:12).
G2487.origine: The word ἴχνος (ichnos) refers to the footprint, to what remains after passage. In classical Greek, it is often used figuratively to denote the example or model to follow. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew words that denote the path or imprint. The image is simple and visual: to see someone's trace is to be able to follow them.
G2487.emploi: The word trace appears three times in the New Testament, always figuratively. In Romans 4:12, Paul uses it to speak of those who follow Abraham's example of faith in uncircumcision. In 2 Corinthians 12:18, it denotes the common manner of conduct, the same shared spirit of action. In 1 Peter 2:21, it carries the strongest meaning: believers are called to follow the example of the suffering Christ. The word trace never appears in its literal and concrete sense (physical imprint) in the New Testament: it is constantly used as an image of spiritual imitation.
G2487.portee: This word invites the believer to a concrete imitation: to follow the traces of Christ means to walk where He walked, to reproduce His love and sacrifice. It is also a call to imitate the saints and those who have faith — not a servile imitation, but a stepping into a proven path. This reminds us that the Christian life is not abstract: it must produce visible acts, observable conduct, like traces that can be followed.

sens: King of Judah, son and successor of King Uzziah
G2488.detail: Joatham is a king of the kingdom of Judah in the royal lineage of Israel. He is the son of King Uzziah and the father of King Ahaz. The Bible mentions him in the genealogy of Jesus Christ reported by Matthew, where he occupies his rightful place as a link in the genealogical chain connecting David to Jesus.
G2488.origine: The name Joatham comes from the Hebrew Yotham (יוֹתָם), composed of two elements: "Yo" (abbreviation of the divine Name) and "tham" (perfection or integrity). His name thus means "God is perfect" or "God is upright." It is a typical theophoric name of royalty in Judah.
G2488.emploi: Joatham appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 1:9, in the genealogy of Jesus. This unique mention shows that Matthew includes Joatham among the important kings of Judah who are part of the genealogical tree leading to the Messiah. Although the New Testament recounts nothing of his life or reign, his mention confirms his royal status and his role in the history of God's people.
G2488.portee: The presence of Joatham in the genealogy of Jesus reminds us that Christ descends from the entire royal lineage of Judah, including its ordinary kings and regular successions. It affirms the continuity of the divine promise to the house of David, and that Jesus is part of the real history of Israel, with its successive generations.

sens: Jewish woman who followed Jesus and assisted Him with her resources
Woman present at the resurrection and witness of the angelic appearance
G2489.detail:
1. Jeanne was the wife of Chuza, steward of the tetrarch Herod, and she was part of the group of women who accompanied Jesus during His ministry in Galilee, providing Him with material help and financial support (Luke 8:3). She likely had some means due to her husband's position at the Herodian court.

2. Jeanne was one of the women who went to the tomb after the resurrection of Jesus and who received the announcement of His resurrection from the angels; she testified to the apostles alongside Mary Magdalene and the other disciples (Luke 24:10). Thus, she is among the first witnesses of the Resurrection.
G2489.origine: The name Jeanne is the Greek form of the Aramaic name Iohanan, which means "God is gracious" or "Yahweh has had mercy." This name was borne by several important figures in Israel, including John the Baptist. The Aramaic Iohanan appears in the Greek Old Testament translated as Greek Iōanna.
G2489.emploi: Jeanne appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in the Gospel of Luke. First mentioned in Luke 8:3, she is presented as one of the wealthy women who accompanied Jesus and provided for His material needs during His ministry. Then, in Luke 24:10, she is named among the witnesses of the Resurrection. Luke seems to pay particular attention to Jeanne, distinguishing her by name and social status, which underscores the importance of women's roles in the history of salvation.
G2489.portee: Jeanne illustrates how women of faith, despite their social status or family responsibilities, chose to follow Jesus and contribute to His ministry. Her testimony of the Resurrection reminds us that the first proclaimers of the Gospel, those who saw and heard first, included women honored for their faith and fidelity.

sens: ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of Luke
G2490.detail: Joanan is an ancestor of Jesus mentioned in the genealogy that traces back from Jesus to Adam. He is presented as the son of Rhesa and the father of Joanan according to Luke's genealogy (Luke 3:27). This genealogy outlines the royal and Davidic lineage of Jesus, showing how the Messiah fits into the history of God's people from the origins of humanity.
G2490.origine: The name Joanan comes from the Hebrew Yohanan (יוֹחָנָן), which means "the Lord is merciful." It is a name borne by several important figures in the Old Testament and the Second Temple period. The name expresses the belief that God is capable of showing His grace and compassion.
G2490.emploi: Joanan appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:27, as a link in the genealogical chain connecting Jesus to His ancestors. In this genealogy specific to Luke, Joanan is situated at a time after the Babylonian exile, in the Davidic royal line. His role is simply to pass on the lineage to Jesus, with no biographical details provided.
G2490.portee: This mention of Joanan reminds the reader that Jesus is part of a real and historical genealogy. It affirms that the Messiah did not appear out of nowhere, but is the culmination of a long history of divine faithfulness to the chosen people, from the time of Abraham to His coming.

sens: John the Baptist, preacher who baptized Jesus in the Jordan
John the Apostle, son of Zebedee, one of the twelve disciples of Jesus
The father of Simon Peter, also called Jonah
John, also known as Mark, companion of Paul
The traditional author of Revelation
G2491G.detail:
1. John the Baptist is the preacher who appears at the beginning of Jesus' public life. He preaches repentance in the wilderness of Judea and baptizes the crowds in the Jordan (Matthew 3:1). John affirms his role as the forerunner: "I baptize you with water; but he who is mightier than I is coming" (Luke 3:16). He is arrested and executed by Herod after daring to condemn Herod's marriage to his brother's wife (Matthew 14:4).
2. John the Apostle is one of the twelve disciples called directly by Jesus. Son of Zebedee with his brother James, he is present at key moments in Jesus' ministry and becomes, after Pentecost, a pillar of the Church (Matthew 4:21; Acts 1:13).
3. John is also the name of the father of Simon Peter (John 1:42-43). Jesus calls him Cephas or Peter and establishes a special relationship with him based on love (John 21:15-17).
4. John, also known as Mark, is a young companion of Paul and Barnabas on their early missionary journeys, although he temporarily abandons them (Acts 12:12; 13:5).
5. According to tradition, the Apostle John is also the author of Revelation, the collection of visions he receives on the island of Patmos (Revelation 1:1).
G2491G.origine: The Greek name Ἰωάννης (Iōannēs) is the Hellenized form of the Hebrew word יוֹחָנָן (Yôḥānān), which means "God has been gracious." This name contains the divine element "Yahu" (God) and the idea of grace or mercy. It was common among Jews of the Second Temple and appears in several Greek forms in the Septuagint. The name carries a profession of faith: the one who bears it is marked by God's favor.
G2491G.emploi: The name John appears 87 times in the New Testament, primarily in the four Gospels and Acts. The majority of occurrences refer to John the Baptist, whose forerunner mission dominates the early chapters of the Gospels (Matthew 3-4, Mark 1, Luke 3, John 1). Disciples and crowds wonder if John himself is the Messiah (Luke 3:15), given his significant impact. After his death, his memory and authority remain alive in people's minds (Mark 11:30-32). The Apostle John is mentioned several times among the Twelve and becomes an important figure in Jesus' inner circle. Acts and the epistles also mention John, also known as Mark. The context always indicates which John is being referred to: the Baptist, the apostle son of Zebedee, or the father of Peter.
G2491G.portee: The name John, meaning "God has been gracious," reminds the reader that all those who bear this name in the Gospel are witnesses of divine grace. John the Baptist, despite his prestige, humbly acknowledges that he is not worthy of the coming Messiah: he embodies self-effacement in the presence of Jesus. The Apostle John becomes a model of a beloved and faithful disciple. These accounts invite us to see how God chooses and shapes men to bear witness to His salvation, and how this grace is manifested in self-denial and love.

sens: The Apostle John, son of Zebedee, one of the twelve disciples of Jesus
A cousin or relative of Jesus, father of the Apostle James the Less
The Baptist, forerunner of Jesus
John Mark, companion of Paul
The traditional author of Revelation
G2491H.detail: 1. John is the apostle son of Zebedee, brother of James, one of the three closest disciples of Jesus. Mark tells us that Jesus nicknamed the two brothers "Boanerges," meaning "sons of thunder" (Mark 3:17), perhaps reflecting their fiery temperament. He is among the privileged witnesses: he witnesses the transfiguration (Luke 9:28) and the agony in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). In Acts, he is seen alongside Peter: together they heal the lame man at the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3:1-4) and appear before the Sanhedrin (Acts 4:13). 2. A John is mentioned as the father of the Apostle Peter in the Gospel of John (John 1:42 according to the source definition). 3. John the Baptist appears at the beginning of the story of Jesus, as the forerunner who baptizes with water and prepares the way for the Messiah. 4. John Mark (also called Mark) is a companion of the apostles, notably of Paul and Barnabas in their missions (Acts 12:12, 13:5). 5. Revelation is traditionally attributed to a John who receives the vision of the glorified Church and eschatological events (Revelation 1:1, 22:8).
G2491H.origine: The Greek name "Ἰωάννης" (Iōannēs) comes from the Hebrew "יוֹחָנָן" (Yohanan), which literally means "God has shown favor" or "God has been gracious." The Hebrew root is formed from "Yah" (abbreviation of Yahweh, the divine name) and "hanan" (to show grace, pity). It is a common theophoric name in ancient Israel, carrying a promise of divine blessing. The Greek form is a faithful Hellenization of the Semitic name, adapted to the language of the early Hellenistic Christians.
G2491H.emploi: John is one of the most frequently used names in the New Testament, appearing about 36 times. It primarily refers to John the Apostle, son of Zebedee, who appears from the beginning of the Gospel (Matthew 4:21, Mark 1:19) and throughout Jesus' ministry. He is often associated with Peter and James at key moments: the transfiguration, the Garden of Olives, the miracles. After the resurrection, John remains a pillar of the Jerusalem Church (Galatians 2:9) and is distinguished by his role alongside Peter in Acts (3:1-4:13). His name also appears in the introduction of Revelation (1:1, 1:4) as the one who receives the written vision. The context indicates that he is a major apostolic figure, often referred to as "the disciple whom Jesus loved" in Christian tradition.
G2491H.portee: John embodies the model of the disciple surrendered to Jesus: a humble fisherman, he becomes one of the three closest to the Lord. His journey shows that Jesus chooses ordinary men and transforms them into powerful witnesses of the Gospel. John's faithfulness until death (according to tradition) and his long ministry inspire believers to persevere in love for Christ and service to the Church.

sens: John the Baptist, preacher who baptized in the Jordan
John the apostle, son of Zebedee, disciple of Jesus
The father of Simon Peter
John surnamed Mark, companion of Paul
The author of Revelation
G2491I.detail: 1. John the Baptist is the preacher who announced the coming of Christ and baptized those who repented in the Jordan (Matthew 3:1). 2. John the apostle, son of Zebedee, is one of the twelve closest apostles to Jesus, present at key moments of His ministry (Matthew 4:21). 3. There is also a John who was the father of Simon Peter, who was also an apostle, questioned by Jesus specifically after the resurrection (John 1:43). 4. John surnamed Mark is a companion of Paul and Barnabas in the early missionary journeys of the Church (Acts 12:12). 5. Finally, the author of Revelation identifies himself as John, traditionally identified with the apostle John son of Zebedee (Revelation 1:1).
G2491I.origine: The name John comes from the Hebrew Yohanan, which means "God is gracious" or "God has shown grace." It is a name borne by several important figures in the Old Testament. When the Greek text of the New Testament uses this name, it adapts it to the Greek form Iōannēs, showing how Hebrew names were Hellenized for Greek-speaking readers.
G2491I.emploi: The name Iōannēs designates five distinct individuals in the New Testament. John the Baptist is the most well-known at the beginning of the Gospel, announcing the Messiah. John the apostle, son of Zebedee, frequently appears in the four Gospels and Acts as one of the most important disciples. John the father of Peter is mentioned in John 1:43 and 21:15-17. John surnamed Mark is a missionary companion in Acts 12:12. Finally, the author of Revelation presents himself as John in Revelation 1:1 and 1:4. Each of these individuals plays a specific role in the history of the New Testament and the early Church. Tradition often identifies the apostle John with the author of Revelation, although this is a debated issue.
G2491I.portee: These different Johns illustrate the diversity of witnesses to Christ in the New Testament. John the Baptist prepares the people to recognize Jesus. The apostle John is presented as one who knew Jesus intimately and bears witness to Him. For today's Christian, these names remind us that God used different people to reveal His plan, and that divine grace — signified by the name John itself — is extended to those who serve in humility and faithfulness.

sens: Companion of the apostles Paul and Barnabas on their early missionary journeys
G2491J.detail: John, also called Mark, is a young man who accompanies Paul and Barnabas on their journeys to proclaim the Gospel. He is initially presented as an assistant (Acts 13:5), but he suddenly abandons the mission at Perga and returns to Jerusalem (Acts 13:13), causing tension between Barnabas and Paul (Acts 15:37). He is the same man whom his mother Mary hosts at her home in Jerusalem, where believers gather for prayer (Acts 12:12).
G2491J.origine: Ἰωάννης is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Yohanan, which means "the Lord has shown grace." Mark is a second Latin name adopted by this same John, likely due to his contacts with the Greco-Roman world. This dual naming was common among Hellenized Jews in the first century.
G2491J.emploi: John (Mark) appears exclusively in the book of Acts, in chapter 12 and following, in connection with the missionary journeys. He is first the aide of Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13:5), then abandons the group at Perga (Acts 13:13), which becomes a point of friction during the planning of a second journey (Acts 15:37). These brief mentions show a young man who is unreliable at first, but later Christian tradition recognizes him as having a major role (composition of the Gospel according to Mark).
G2491J.portee: The story of John Mark illustrates how God grants a second chance and transforms failures into lasting service. His initial abandonment of the journey did not close the door to future ministry, reminding believers that hesitant beginnings do not exclude future faithfulness.

sens: father of Simon Peter, the apostle of Jesus
G2491K.detail: Jonah is the father of Simon Peter, the disciple whom Jesus renamed Cephas (Peter). In the Gospel of John, Jesus addresses Simon several times as "Simon, son of Jonah" (John 1:42; John 21:15-17). This patronymic simply indicates lineage: Jonah is Peter's natural father.
G2491K.origine: The Greek name Ἰωνᾶς (Iônas) transcribes the Hebrew name יוֹנָה (Yonah). In Hebrew, this name literally means "dove." It is a common name in ancient Judaism. This Jonah, father of Peter, should not be confused with the prophet Jonah from the book of the same name in the Old Testament: they are two distinct individuals, although they bear the same name.
G2491K.emploi: The name Jonah appears four times in the New Testament, exclusively in John. It is always to designate the father of Simon Peter. Jesus uses it three times during Peter's restoration after the resurrection (John 21:15-17), as if to establish the complete identity of His disciple. This repetition of the patronymic perhaps emphasizes the importance of the moment when Jesus restores Peter's pastoral mission.
G2491K.portee: By naming Peter by his patronymic, Jesus designates him in his entirety — not only by his nickname of rock, but by his family identity. This reminds us that Jesus knows each of His disciples not merely as a function or a nickname, but in their complete reality, their origins, their history.

sens: Man of the Old Testament famous for his patience in the face of suffering
G2492.detail: Job is a biblical character whose story is told throughout the book that bears his name. He is presented as a righteous and faithful man who experienced terrible trials: the loss of his children, his possessions, and a severe illness. Despite everything, he maintained his trust in God — this is what the Bible calls his "patience." James 5:11 cites him as an example to encourage Christians who suffer: they must endure in faith, as Job did, knowing that God is "full of mercy and compassion" and that He has a good end for those who persevere.
G2492.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew אִיּוֹב (Job), whose exact meaning remains debated by scholars. It could mean "one who returns" or "the hostile" depending on the roots one emphasizes. Job is best known as the hero of the book of Job, one of the great poems of wisdom in the Old Testament.
G2492.emploi: Job appears only once in the New Testament, in James 5:11, where the apostle James mentions him as a model of perseverance in suffering. This shows that, at the time of the New Testament, the story of Job was well known among believers and served as encouragement for those going through trials. It is a concrete example of God's faithfulness to those who persevere.
G2492.portee: The name of Job reminds the reader that in Christ, one cannot escape suffering, but it is never sterile or meaningless. It becomes an opportunity to see the character of God — His mercy, justice, love — and to grow in faith. For the suffering Christian, Job is a witness that God does not abandon him and that a deep joy awaits him.

sens: Prophet of the Old Testament
Author of the prophetic book that bears his name
G2493.detail: Joel is an Israelite prophet whose message has been preserved in a book of the Old Testament. On the day of Pentecost, Peter quotes Joel's prophecy about the outpouring of the Holy Spirit: "This is what was spoken by the prophet Joel" (Acts 2:16). This prophetic passage speaks of the time when God would pour out His Spirit on all flesh, which is precisely fulfilled with the disciples filled with the Holy Spirit in Jerusalem.
G2493.origine: The name Joel comes from the Hebrew Yoel, composed of two elements: Yo (an abbreviation of the divine name YHWH) and El (God). The name thus means "YHWH is God" or "God is Yahweh." It is a typical theophoric name in Israel, affirming the divinity of the God of Israel. Joel was a prophet of Israel, and the exact date of his ministry is unknown, but his book has been preserved in the canon of the Old Testament.
G2493.emploi: Joel appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 2:16, where Peter invokes him as a prophetic source. The prophet Joel is cited to show that the miraculous events of Pentecost—the gift of the Holy Spirit accompanied by supernatural phenomena—constitute the fulfillment of an ancient promise of Israel. This citation establishes a direct link between the Old and New Testaments, showing that the coming of the Holy Spirit had long been foretold by the prophets.
G2493.portee: The mention of Joel reminds the reader that God's plan spans the centuries: what was fulfilled at Pentecost was not a surprise, but the realization of a promise made centuries earlier. For the believer, this affirms that God is faithful and that His Word never changes, from the first to the last testament.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy according to Luke
G2494.detail: Jonam is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in Luke 3:30. He appears in the genealogy that Luke traces from Jesus back to Adam. Jonam is presented as the son of Eliakim and the father of Joseph (the supposed father of Jesus according to the flesh).
G2494.origine: The name Jonam (Greek Ἰωνάν) is the Greek equivalent of a Hebrew name. It appears exclusively in Luke's genealogy, which traces the ancestors of Jesus through the line of Nathan, son of David.
G2494.emploi: Jonam is cited only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:30. He appears in the general genealogy of Jesus Christ that the apostle Luke establishes by tracing back from Jesus to Adam. His role is purely genealogical: he represents a link in the chain of generations leading to Jesus.

sens: Hebrew prophet of the 8th century B.C.
Figure of resurrection and judgment
Prophetic sign of Jesus
G2495H.detail:
1. Jonah is a Hebrew prophet of the Old Testament, known for being sent to preach repentance to Nineveh, the capital of Assyria. In the New Testament, Jesus mentions him as a recognized authority of his time (Matthew 12:41).

2. The miracle of Jonah—three days in the belly of a great fish—becomes for Jesus an image of his own resurrection: "just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of a great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth" (Matthew 12:40). This is the only "sign" that Jesus promises to an unbelieving generation.

3. Jesus contrasts the quick repentance of the Ninevites—who converted at Jonah's preaching—with the unbelief of his contemporaries: the men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment to condemn this generation (Matthew 12:41). Jonah thus embodies the power of the divine word to transform and the judgment that weighs on those who refuse to hear it.
G2495H.origine: The Hebrew name יוֹנָה (Yonah) literally means "dove," a symbol of purity and simplicity—it is the image of a humble prophet, despite his initial resistance to God's call. The historical figure is described in the book of Jonah in the Old Testament. Jesus and his contemporaries were well acquainted with this book and the teaching it contains about divine mercy and conversion.
G2495H.emploi: Jesus cites Jonah six times in a few verses (Matthew 12:39-41, 16:4; Luke 11:29-30, 32), always in the context of a request for a miraculous sign. The Pharisees and scribes demand a miracle to believe in him, and Jesus refuses: he will give "no other sign than that of Jonah" (Matthew 12:39). This miracle—the living emergence from the fish after three days—foreshadows his own emergence from the tomb. Luke adds a nuance: Jonah was himself "a sign" for the Ninevites, just as the death and resurrection of Jesus will be the definitive sign for this generation (Luke 11:30). Jonah thus appears as a key to understanding the paschal mystery.
G2495H.portee: For the believer, Jonah teaches that the supreme sign of Jesus' identity is not a spectacular wonder, but his resurrection. It also shows that in response to the divine preaching, two paths open: that of the repentance of the Ninevites, or that of judgment. The mention of Jonah invites us to examine our own response to God's call.

sens: King of Judah, son of Jehoshaphat and father of Uzziah, in the genealogy of Jesus
G2496.detail: 1. Joram (or Jehoram) is a king of Judah who appears in the genealogy of Jesus presented by Matthew. He is mentioned between Jehoshaphat and Uzziah (Matthew 1:8). This ancestor of Jesus is part of the royal line of Judah, which emphasizes that Jesus descends from the house of David.
G2496.origine: The name Joram comes from the Hebrew יוֹרָם (Yôrâm), composed of two elements: "Yô" (an abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh) and "rîm" ("to raise" or "to exalt"). The name thus means "Yahweh raises" or "Yahweh is exalted." It is a common theophoric name among the kings of Israel and Judah.
G2496.emploi: Joram appears only once in the New Testament, in chapter 1 of Matthew, in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:8). This genealogy traces the descent of Jesus from Abraham and David to his birth. Joram represents one of the intermediate generations of the royal line of Judah. His inclusion in this genealogy shows that Jesus comes from real earthly kings before becoming the eternal King.
G2496.portee: The appearance of Joram in the genealogy of Jesus reminds us that Jesus is situated in the concrete history of the people of Judah and its royalty. This confirms that Jesus truly came from the house of David, thus fulfilling the messianic promises of the Old Testament. It is a detail that anchors faith in Jesus in historical reality and in divine promises.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy of Luke
G2497.detail: Jorim is a biblical proper name that appears only once in the Gospel of Luke, in the midst of the genealogy of Jesus. He is an ancestor of Jesus according to the genealogical chain of Mary (or Joseph according to interpretations), situated about fifteen centuries before Christ. In the list of Luke 3:29, Jorim is presented as the father of Matthat and the son of Eliezer.
G2497.origine: The name "Jorim" is of Hebrew origin (אִיוֹרִים, Iōreim). It would mean "the Lord exalts" or "God raises." It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God and expresses trust in His action. In the Old Testament, several variants of this type of name express exaltation and honor given to God.
G2497.emploi: Jorim appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 3:29. It is in the genealogy that Luke provides of Jesus, which is different from that of Matthew. Luke traces back to Adam and presents the descent through several generations to show that Jesus is truly the Son of Man and the heir of all humanity. Jorim occupies a modest yet real position in this chain, as a link between Eliezer and Matthat, thus contributing to the genealogical legitimacy of the Messiah.
G2497.portee: The mention of Jorim, although unique and brief, reminds the reader that Jesus is situated in a real history, with named and counted ancestors. Luke establishes that the Messiah is not a mythological figure detached from humanity, but a son of Abraham and David, rooted in the genealogy and history of the people of God. This is an affirmation of the real incarnation of Christ.

sens: King of the kingdom of Judah in the Davidic dynasty
G2498.detail: Josaphat is a king of Judah, mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1:8. He is the son of Asa and the father of Joram, which shows his central place in the royal lineage of Judah that led to the birth of the Messiah.
G2498.origine: The name Josaphat comes from the Hebrew Jehoshaphat, composed of two elements: Yaho (a shortened form of the divine name) and Shaphat ("to judge"). The name thus means "God judges" or "may God judge." This name reflects the trust that his parents placed in God as the sovereign judge.
G2498.emploi: Josaphat is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 1:8, in the genealogy of Jesus that traces back to David. This mention situates him as an important link in the chain of kings of Judah from which the Messiah came. He is a historical king, well documented in the books of Kings in the Old Testament, where his reign and religious reforms are described.
G2498.portee: For the Christian reader, Josaphat represents a link in the royal genealogy that confirms that Jesus is indeed the heir of the promise made to David. His presence in this genealogical list reminds us that Jesus was born into an authentic royal family, rooted in the real history of Israel.
